chunks: "Flyback voltage, or inductive kick, is the voltage spike you get when you suddenly interrupt the current through an inductor, like a motor or solenoid coil.
An inductor's voltage is L times di dt. While the switch is on, the coil has current I and stores half L I squared of energy in its magnetic field.
When you open the switch, the current wants to keep flowing, so the coil generates whatever voltage it needs, with the polarity reversed, to push the current through.

With nothing to take the current, that voltage shoots up until something conducts: the switch avalanches, an arc forms across relay contacts, or the parasitic capacitance charges up to hundreds or thousands of volts.
The fix is to give the current a path. The standard solution is a flyback or freewheel diode across the coil, reverse-biased in normal operation.
When the switch opens, the diode conducts and the current recirculates through the coil and diode, so the switch only sees the supply plus a diode drop.
The downside is that the current decays slowly, since the only voltage opposing it is the diode drop.
If you need fast release, you add a Zener or TVS in series with the diode, a snubber, or an active clamp, at the price of a higher switch voltage.
I'd also mention it's not the same as a flyback converter, which uses the same effect on purpose in a transformer-based supply."
